The weather pattern, known as a Dana, occurs most often in autumn.

Models show more than 100mm of rain could fall across the region on Friday, with 200-300mm possible in some areas. Cities including Valencia and Castelló de la Plana, are most at risk. items.content_html: Trucks, farms and industry are powered with diesel. Now prices are soaring due to refinery disruptions, supply shortages and geopolitical tensions. A potential US export ban could make Europe's diesel crunch even worse.

items.title: Will Jürgen Klopp's charisma be enough for Germany?
items.content_html: After defeat to Greece, Jürgen Klopp faces the first real test of his tenure as coach of Germany's national men's football team. Can his charisma alone push this group forward?

items.title: Ireland beat Israel 3-0 in Nations League match overshadowed by political controversy
items.content_html: Ireland easily beat Israel in a Nations League fixture that 24 hours earlier appeared in doubt. One Irish player pulled out of the match to express his opposition to Israel's actions in the Gaza Strip.

items.title: What would Francis of Assisi make of his fame today?
items.content_html: The Catholic saint renounced wealth and fame to become a mendicant friar. Yet throughout history, his teachings and life have inspired popes, Dante and even Mussolini.

items.title: Germany news: Are Germans giving up their beloved meat and sausages?
items.content_html: Germans used to be all about sausages and meat. While those do remain popular, things seem to be slowly changing. There also are new insights into the economic side of East Germany's espionage DW has more.

items.title: Backlash over data centers tests Europe's AI ambitions
items.content_html: Massive data centers needed to run AI are triggering protests across Europe. Their operators counter that they boost digital sovereignty and energy independence.

items.title: DW shows solidarity with Georgians' commitment to democracy
items.content_html: Cultural and media professionals in Georgia remain under threat. A DW panel brings together insiders who share their hopes and fears.

items.title: Bundesliga, other top European leagues call for major FIFA reforms
items.content_html: The Bundesliga and three other leading European football leagues have said major reforms to world-governing body FIFA are "essential." However, they stopped short of calling for the resignation of boss Gianni Infantino.

items.title: Jürgen Klopp starts Germany job with shaky Netherlands draw
items.content_html: A late Netherlands goal denied Jürgen Klopp a win in his first match as Germany coach. The former Liverpool and Borussia Dortmund boss has big ambitions, but the game showed he's going to need more time to achieve them.

items.title: Three-way battle for power in world chess: Who will be elected FIDE president in Samarkand?
items.content_html: The era of Russian presidents is coming to an end at the World Chess Federation (FIDE). Two Germans and one Kazakh are up for election. Among the issues at play are money, Kremlin influence, and unanswered questions.

items.title: After several difficult years, economists now expect German economy to grow
items.content_html: Germany's economy is growing again, but recovery remains on shaky ground. High government spending is keeping the economy afloat, while energy prices, a shortage of skilled workers and debt continue to weigh on it.

items.title: Political psychology: Why extremist parties are thriving and what democratic politicians can do against it
items.content_html: Far-right and far-left parties are celebrating success after success, leaving moderate politicians in the dust and worrying many Germans. Political psychology helps us understand what's behind growing polarization.

items.title: Could flattering AI make humanity turn on itself?
items.content_html: A study shows chatbots mirror users' politics, part of a broader tendency known as AI sycophancy. Researchers fear this could deepen polarization.

items.title: Germany news: Berlin officially withdraws Olympics bid
items.content_html: Berlin's decision to withdraw its Olympic bid means that only Munich and the western Rhine/Ruhr region are left in the running as potential Olympic hosts. DW has more.

items.title: Could a Left Party government in Berlin expropriate large real estate companies?
items.content_html: The socialist Left Party won the Berlin election partly on the promise to implement the city's 2021 expropriation referendum as a way to solve the city's rent crisis. But can it really happen?

items.title: China's 13-year-old swimming star raises questions on child athletes
items.content_html: Three gold medals and three Asian Games records have catapulted China's Yu Zidi, 13, into the sporting spotlight. She is far from the first teen prodigy, but should teens be competing at elite level?

items.title: Germany's oldest party, the center-left SPD, is in a difficult position following its success in the Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania state election
items.content_html: Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) has vowed to press ahead with controversial reforms, but resistance is mounting within his coalition partner, the SPD. How much dissent can a governing coalition tolerate?

items.title: Munich and Cologne-Rhine-Ruhr – Germany's two remaining Olympic candidates
items.content_html: Munich or the Cologne-Rhine-Ruhr region? Germany aims to host the Olympic Games again. Just two candidates are left after Berlin pulled out at the last minute.

items.title: El Nino explained: How the weather pattern affects hurricanes and tropical storms
items.content_html: From drought to major floods and extreme heat, El Nino will have a huge impact on the world's weather. In the Atlantic, it could mean a season without hurricanes.

items.title: China's new travel rules unsettle tech giants and talent
items.content_html: Beijing is locking the gates to stop expertise and capital in strategic industries from fleeing. The country accused of industrial-scale intellectual property theft now fears the West will take its own.

items.title: Living in the shadow of LA's hidden oil wells
items.content_html: Many lifelong residents of Los Angeles have health impacts from growing up close to oil extraction. Now, the city is trying to close down the worst offenders, but it's an enormous task.

items.title: Could we see MMA at the Olympics?
items.content_html: Mixed martial arts has made its debut at the Asian Games this week. It takes the sport closer to the Olympics, but there are doubts about the next step — and the influence of the popular and lucrative UFC.

items.title: Male infertility is 'grossly underreported'
items.content_html: It's not all on women anymore — doctors do test men for sperm count and motility. But still too few men get checked, possibly due to a misconception that a healthy sex life means healthy sperm. Spoiler: It doesn't.

items.title: Will Germany have enough gas this winter amid energy supply crunch?
items.content_html: Germany's gas storage sites are far less full than in recent years. Officials say supplies are secure, but analysts warn that a cold winter or import disruptions could push prices higher. So how secure is the supply?

items.title: Princess Diana's brother makes explosive claims about royals in new memoir
items.content_html: Here are some of the key revelations from Charles Earl Spencer's highly anticipated memoir "Swan Song: Diana, My Sister." It has already provoked Buckingham Palace to react.

items.title: Germany's car crisis: Can the 35-hour workweek survive?
items.content_html: German carmakers want employees to work 40 hours instead of the current 35 without extra pay, arguing it would improve competitiveness. Unions strongly oppose the proposal and view it as an attack on workers' rights.

items.title: Germany faces energy tax losses as EV sales rise
items.content_html: The rapid shift to electric vehicles in Germany is cutting fuel tax revenue for the government. As EV sales surge, policymakers face growing pressure to find new ways to fund roads and transportation infrastructure.

items.title: Summer of 2026 broke records in Europe, and caused deaths
items.content_html: The summer of 2026 was not only the hottest on record in Europe, it also saw a record number of people die. More than 16,000 are thought to have died because of the heat in Germany alone.

items.title: Oktoberfest 2026: Everything you need to know
items.content_html: This year, AI will be used to manage overcrowded situations. Find all the numbers surrounding the fest — including the price of water!

items.title: Rebels, workers, radicals: The making of 'Red Berlin'
items.content_html: Bloody May, student sit-ins and the squatter movement: Berlin has long been a hotbed for working-class organizing and radical left-wing politics.

items.title: Women's football in Germany booming, but still much to do
items.content_html: Women's football is growing rapidly, particularly in Germany. Nevertheless, equal pay and investment remain major talking points.

items.title: Strait of Hormuz attacks spill oil into Persian Gulf
items.content_html: As war disrupts one of the world's busiest shipping lanes, satellite images reveal that oil is spreading toward protected coral reefs and mangrove forests.

items.title: Dual citizenship means Germany now in competition for talent
items.content_html: Coach Jürgen Klopp has named several players to his first Germany squad who are eligible to play for other countries. Some still aren't committed to playing for thje national team long-term.

items.title: Beethoven and Andy Warhol: Rebel icons on show in Bonn
items.content_html: The new exhibition "Beethoven by Warhol" at the Beethoven House in Bonn presents the pop artist's late masterpiece: a picture of Ludwig van Beethoven. The exhibition shares the story of the work with the public.

items.title: VAR's mission creep a problem for football
items.content_html: After a decade of use, questions around VAR in football are louder than ever. Has the technology strayed too far from its remit?

items.title: Alexander Ovechkin backs Putin party in campaign video
items.content_html: Ice hockey legend Alexander Ovechkin has lent Vladimir Putin's party a helping hand in its parliamentary election campaign. That's in keeping with a pattern of support by an athlete who claims not to be political.

items.title: Klopp wants Germany's football team to 'reclaim the flag'
items.content_html: Jürgen Klopp, Germany's new head coach, says he wants his team to reclaim pride in being German after recent political developments.

items.title: Jews once lived lived here: When houses tell stories
items.content_html: Time and again, residents tracing the history of their homes discover the lives of Jewish predecessors who fled or were deported amid stories of suffering and loss.

items.title: Jürgen Klopp's first Germany squad includes 44 players
items.content_html: Germany's new head coach Jürgen Klopp has named a huge squad for his first four games, splitting them into two groups. A host of new faces is included.

items.title: Saint, sinner or feminist icon: How Mary Magdalene's image evolved through time
items.content_html: From "Apostle of the Apostles" to prostitute, Mary Magdalene has been assigned a wide variety of roles, as a new exhibition shows.

items.title: How climate change worsened Nepal's deadly mountain collapse
items.content_html: A glacier and rock collapse in Nepal killed nearly 1,400 people and left thousands missing. Scientists say decades of warming helped set the disaster in motion.

items.title: Global Gender Gap Report: Women's hard-won gains 'fragile'
items.content_html: Two decades of progress toward gender parity is at risk as women's political representation declines, according to a new World Economic Forum report. At the current pace, the remaining gap could take 120 years to close.

items.title: German drama 'Blindspot Berlin' revisits 2016 Christmas market attack
items.content_html: A decade after the terrorist attack on a Berlin Christmas market, a new German miniseries looks into the institutional failures that allowed the deadly truck rampage to happen.

items.title: How extreme heat is hitting wallets
items.content_html: Heat waves, wildfires and floods have cascading economic impacts, causing incomes to decline and the price of basic goods to rise. The trend will escalate as temperatures continue to increase.

items.title: Spanish scientists find first evidence of Diplodocus dinosaur in Europe
items.content_html: Paleontologists in Spain say they have found the first evidence of the long-necked Diplodocus genus of dinosaur outside of North America. They found bones at the rich La Tejeria fossil site in Teruel in eastern Spain.

items.title: Why the era of cheap government debt is over
items.content_html: US debt has topped $40 trillion. How risky is the country's growing debt burden. And will investors keep funding Washington's deficits?

items.title: Why AI researchers warn humanity could face extinction
items.content_html: Could artificial intelligence pose an existential threat to humanity? Some leading researchers are warning against an unregulated race toward AI superintelligence.

items.title: Iran and US: Two countries and the pistachio between them
items.content_html: The pistachios sold across the United States have a surprising history: California's trees trace their roots to Iran. Now, both regions face the same threat — their farmland is sinking as groundwater disappears.

items.title: Africa's richest man Dangote's IPO out of reach in Nigeria
items.content_html: Dangote seeks $1.6 billion from investors to finance a $14.3 billion expansion and thus double the oil refinery's capacity. The offer could give millions of Nigerians a stake in the company. But who can truly afford it?

items.title: The Crusades: How a medieval holy war still shapes politics
items.content_html: In 1095, the Catholic Church launched the Crusades: wars that left millions dead and whose legacy still shapes political and ideological conflicts.

items.title: Can Iran replace sea trade with land routes?
items.content_html: Iran is shifting trade toward northern ports and land routes as its southern shipping faces a US blockade. Analysts say the corridors can keep essential goods moving, but cannot replace maritime trade.

items.title: Why are European banks moving gold out of United States?
items.content_html: The Netherlands and France have moved their gold out of US vaults. Part of the reason is fears about the reliability of the US, but equally important is the need to keep gold closer to home in the event of a crisis.

items.title: Corals as climate archive: Are El Nino events intensifying?
items.content_html: Records show that El Nino events have been frequent and often extreme over the past few decades. Is this normal? Or is it the result of climate change? Corals can give us a clear indication.

items.title: India looks to steer BRICS away from anti-Western turn
items.content_html: The BRICS summit 2026 takes place in Delhi this weekend. Unlike last year, Putin and Xi are expected to attend. Can India keep the expanded bloc united?

items.title: The 'end of an era' as Goethe-Institut in Russia closes
items.content_html: The Goethe-Institut was one of the last German institutions still operating in Russia. However, following Moscow's decision to close its offices, all employees will have to stop working by September 13.

items.title: How Celine Dion became a pop culture icon across generations
items.content_html: As the global star kicks off her anticipated Paris residency, here's how Celine Dion managed to gain younger followers while keeping her loyal older fans.

items.title: How Belarusians still find hope in a silenced country
items.content_html: The documentary "Letters from the Silenced Country" depicts the ongoing repression under the authoritarian regime. Director Andrei Kutsila talked to DW ahead of the film's Venice premiere.

items.title: Why we're still looking for dark matter
items.content_html: When physicists said they may have spotted evidence of dark matter almost 100 years after it was proposed as a theory, the internet lit up. Here's why we're searching for the thing that holds everything else together.

items.title: Conspiracy theories can provide answers but not peace
items.content_html: Twenty-five years after 9/11, conspiracy theories about the terrorist attacks persist. But even as an attempt to make sense of a tragedy, psychologists say the benefit in conspiracy ideation or belief is short-lived.

items.title: The billion-euro trade driving Europe's eels to extinction
items.content_html: Traffickers are making big bucks smuggling millions of critically endangered eels across continents, using suitcases on planes and legal loopholes to deliver them to dinnerplates. Where are the smuggling hotspots?

items.title: The Bayeux Tapestry in London: What's behind the hype?
items.content_html: The exhibition of the Bayeux Tapestry at the British Museum is eagerly anticipated across the UK, as the medieval masterpiece is considered by many to be a symbol of the country's identity.
